performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
intro: One bassoon note carries Mendelssohn’s concerto into this C-major Andante, where Soojin Han’s violin sings over softly moving strings. In the middle, the same violin must play a melody and its shivering accompaniment at once.

cues.title: The bassoon carries on
cues.text: The first bassoon keeps its B after the first movement ends, then rises a semitone to C. A flute joins it, and the low strings begin to move. That narrow step takes the concerto from E minor into the Andante’s C major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, plate M.B. 18, p. 27, join to the Andante. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song above the strings
cues.text: The violin’s C-major melody stretches over a gently rising and falling string accompaniment. The winds rest through its opening phrases. Mendelssohn leaves the soloist room to sing, with the orchestra moving quietly beneath each held note.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 28: solo melody in C major above pianissimo strings, with the winds initially silent.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Breadth and dignity
cues.text: The Andante has three parts: the violin’s C-major melody, an A-minor middle section and the melody’s return. Donald Tovey finds “true breadth and dignity” in it, and in the middle section “agitation and anxiety” without fussiness.
cues.evidence: Donald Tovey, Essays in Musical Analysis, vol. 3 (Oxford, 1936), pp. 180–181: “The movement has true breadth and dignity”, and its middle episode “achieves a real expression of agitation and anxiety without the fussiness which Mendelssohn was too often apt to express instead”: https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.28887. The three parts: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 28–36: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf

cues.title: No pauses between movements
cues.text: Mendelssohn links all three movements without a break. Weber’s Konzertstück had done something similar, but no work calling itself a concerto had. Steven Ledbetter adds that the Liszt concertos and many others are hard to imagine without it.
cues.evidence: Steven Ledbetter, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note on the Violin Concerto: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: David asks for brilliance
cues.text: David presses Mendelssohn for a concerto and asks that it be brilliant. “How can anyone like me do this?” Mendelssohn answers, and adds that the whole first solo is to lie on the E string. The concerto, promised in 1838, is finished in 1844.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn to Ferdinand David, 1839, as quoted by Marianne Williams Tobias in the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note (“You ask that it should be brilliant, and how can anyone like me do this? The whole of the first solo is to be for the E string”); the letter itself was not opened: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mendelssohn-concerto-in-e-minor/. Steven Ledbetter records David’s urgent pleas that Mendelssohn finish the piece: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: A few days in July
cues.text: In July 1839, Mendelssohn tells Ferdinand David that he needs only “a few days in a good mood” to produce the promised concerto. The days prove elusive. He works seriously on it in July 1844 and finishes the score that September.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn to Ferdinand David, July 1839, quoted by Steven Ledbetter; the same note dates the concentrated work to July–September 1844. https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: One violin, two jobs
cues.text: Trumpets and timpani darken the middle section, in A minor, above trembling strings. When the solo violin takes up the tune, it also supplies the quick repeated notes beneath it. The bow must keep the melody singing while the lower notes shiver.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 31–34. Steven Ledbetter identifies the trumpets, timpani and string tremolos: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto. The soloist’s combined melody and accompaniment is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The middle section drives upward
cues.text: Chord after chord, the orchestra drives the A-minor middle section towards fortissimo, with sforzandi and long crescendos, while the soloist’s shivering semiquavers carry on underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, printed pp. 30–33: crescendos, fortissimo chords and sforzandi over continuous solo semiquavers; the section then falls away (dim., sempre dim.) on p. 34. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song returns in C
cues.text: The violin recovers its first melody in C major. The strings keep a quick, quiet accompaniment beneath it, carrying some of the middle section’s trembling into the return. Flute and clarinet add small answers around the solo line.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 34–35: return of the C-major melody over repeated string notes and woodwind responses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A label for Milstein
cues.text: In March 1948, Columbia librarian Helene F. Chmura signs a label order for ML 4001: Nathan Milstein playing this concerto, with Bruno Walter conducting the New York Philharmonic. The company releases it that June as Columbia launches the long-playing record.
cues.evidence: Amanda Jenkins, Library of Congress, “Inside the Archival Box: The First Long-Playing Disc” (13 April 2019), reproduces the label paperwork signed on 1 March 1948 and gives the June release. https://blogs.loc.gov/now-see-hear/2019/04/inside-the-archival-box-the-first-long-playing-disc/

cues.title: The violin comes down
cues.text: Sempre più piano — softer all the time. The violin’s last runs descend towards a quiet C-major chord, with the strings plucking beneath the final wind notes. A pause is written over the last chord; the next page already has the finale’s linking phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 36–37: sempre più piano, pizzicato strings, final C-major chord with fermata, then Allegretto non troppo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bassoon hands over to the violin
transitions.from: Link · The bassoon’s B rises to C
transitions.to: A · The violin sings in C major
transitions.how: The bassoon’s held B rises to C, carrying the music out of E minor. Flute and other winds begin the Andante over low strings. They fall silent for the violin’s C-major song, leaving the strings’ pianissimo accompaniment to move beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 27–28: sustained bassoon, wind introduction and solo entry.

transitions.title: Trumpets and timpani disturb the song
transitions.from: A · The violin sings in C major
transitions.to: B · Trumpets and timpani in A minor
transitions.how: The strings’ repeated notes swell towards the A-minor middle section. Trumpets and timpani join the wind instruments’ new theme at fortissimo, with the low strings bowing beneath them. The soloist then takes that tune into double-stopping, playing its own quick accompaniment below the melody.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 31–32: fortissimo chord, orchestral theme and the solo violin’s two-part writing.

transitions.title: The violin sings above the tremble
transitions.from: B · Trumpets and timpani in A minor
transitions.how: The violin’s restless double-stopping diminishes, marked sempre diminuendo. The strings take over the quick repeated notes, leaving the soloist free to bring back the C-major melody. The bass reaches C beneath it; flute and clarinet answer softly.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 34–35: diminuendo, transfer of repeated notes to the strings and return of the solo melody.

transitions.title: The violin settles over C
transitions.to: Coda · The violin descends to rest
transitions.how: The solo violin descends through its last runs, sempre più piano. Low C anchors the close while the string parts change to pizzicato and the winds finish their phrases. A C-major chord with a fermata ends the Andante; the following Allegretto non troppo starts in E minor.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 36–37: C-major close and E-minor link.

source.title: Mendelssohn, Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel; Rietz edition, Serie 4 No. 18)
source.locator: II. Andante, pp. 27–36: bassoon link and wind introduction, p. 27; solo song, p. 28; A-minor middle section, pp. 31–34; C-major return and close, pp. 34–36.

timeline.note: The first bassoon holds B across the join between movements, then rises to C.
The flute begins the Andante’s introduction, with other woodwinds and low strings beneath it.
The solo violin sings in C major above gently rising and falling strings.
The orchestra introduces the middle section’s theme at fortissimo; the soloist joins its first chord.
The violin plays the middle section’s melody and its quick repeated accompaniment together.
Trumpets and timpani reinforce the wind chords above trembling strings and the solo violin.
The violin recovers its C-major song above quick, quiet notes in the strings.

composer.epithet: At sixteen, he made eight string players sound like the most exhilarating orchestra in Europe.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Düsseldorf music director, 1833–35; Leipzig Gewandhaus conductor from 1835
Married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children; brother of Fanny Hensel
Leipzig Conservatoire, founded 1843; ten visits to Britain
composer.background:
In 1825, sixteen-year-old Felix Mendelssohn wrote a birthday present for his violin teacher, Eduard Rietz. It required four violins, two violas and two cellos, and gave Rietz a first-violin part that climbs out over the other seven players in long, buoyant arcs. The E♭ major Octet still sounds like someone discovering how much pleasure eight string instruments can make. Eleven years later, its composer played second viola in a public performance. Writing to Karl Klingemann on 31 January 1836, he admitted to “heart palpitations”.

He had been noisy from the start. In 1812, his sister Fanny wrote to friends in Hamburg: “Felix has a strong voice and sings all day.” He was born there on 3 February 1809; the family moved to Berlin two years later. His father Abraham was a banker, his grandfather Moses the Jewish philosopher. Abraham and Lea Mendelssohn had their children baptised as Christians in 1816 and used the additional surname Bartholdy. Fanny and Felix learnt piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter.
